children.name: Project Description
children.reason:
Evaluation of the README file:

project_purpose:
Score (avg): 3.0
[QWEN] The README partially describes the project's purpose but does not adequately explain why it is useful. It identifies the project as the '"EVB-IT digital" contract tool' and explains that "a pre-built, executable HTML file for each, EVB-IT digital Designer and Player is offered in the directory built-html", with links to both files. The "Project Structure" section also clarifies the components (frontend app, build tooling, build script), and the "Building locally" section hints at functionality by describing the outputs (Player mode, Designer mode, a combined version, and a "Prüftool" for inlining into the branded EVB-IT build). However, the README never explains what EVB-IT digital actually is (a standard framework for IT service contracts), what the Designer and Player modes do, or what problem the tool solves for its users (e.g., creating, checking, or evaluating IT service contracts). A first-time reader would understand that the artifact is an HTML tool with two modes, but would not learn what the tool accomplishes or why using it would be beneficial. This is an acceptable but incomplete purpose description.

setup_instructions:
Score (avg): 5.0
[QWEN] The README provides thorough, well-organized setup instructions. It includes a "Prerequisites" section specifying the required toolchain ("To build the app: Node 16, npm 8"), a "Getting Started" section with concrete, copy-pasteable commands (cd app; npm install; npm run dev), and a "Building locally" section explaining how to use the one-command build script (./build.sh), noting that it checks dependencies before building and describing the five expected output files. Additionally, it points to "the application's README (app/README.md) for more detailed building instructions" and includes a full, step-by-step workflow for generating the SBOM (install, prune dev dependencies, run syft, postprocess with python3 build/process_spdx.py). The instructions are specific, ordered, and cover both development and release workflows, making them easy to follow.

info_project_status:
Score (avg): 1.0
[QWEN] The README contains no information about the project's status. There is no statement indicating whether the project is under active development, in maintenance mode, or no longer maintained; no version number or changelog; no links to releases, commits, or a roadmap; and no indication of how frequently updates occur. While the presence of SBOM generation and build tooling might implicitly suggest ongoing engineering work, the README itself never explicitly or implicitly addresses the project's lifecycle status, so a reader cannot determine from this document whether the project is active or abandoned.

info_maintainer:
Score (avg): 1.0
[QWEN] The README contains no information about who maintains or contributes to the project. There is no author name, maintainer list, owning organization or company, contact information (email, issue tracker, discussion forum), or contribution guidelines. While the name "EVB-IT" suggests a connection to the German IT industry association, the document never explicitly attributes the project to a person or organization, and there is no "Contributing," "Support," or "Contact" section. Therefore, a reader cannot identify who is responsible for the project or how to contribute to or seek help with it.

children.name: Project Structure
children.reason:
Project structure evaluation:

directory_organization:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] Question evaluated: Does the project follow appropriate directory organization conventions for its technology stack (Vue 3 + Vite + TypeScript + Cypress + Storybook)? The layout is highly conventional: the application lives in app/ with src/, public/, entry HTML files at the app root (index.html, creator.html, player.html, verification.html) correctly paired with matching entry points (main.ts, main-creator.ts, main-player.ts, main-verification.ts) — proper Vite multi-page-app convention. Tooling configs are where Vite/Vue projects expect them (vite.config.ts, tsconfig.json plus tsconfig.app/node/test.json, tailwind.config.js, postcss.config.js, .eslintrc.cjs, .prettierrc.json, .ncurc.json, cypress.config.ts). Cypress follows the modern v10+ structure (cypress/e2e, cypress/fixtures, cypress/support, cypress/tsconfig.json), Storybook lives in .storybook/, dependency patches in patches/ (patch-package convention), build helpers in scripts/, and git hooks in .husky/. Unit tests are co-located as *.spec.ts, which is the accepted Vitest/Vue convention rather than a legacy top-level tests/ directory. Deductions keep this at 4 rather than 5: there is no docs/ directory (documentation is only README.md at root and in app/); built-html/ contains committed pre-built artifacts (EVB-IT_digital_Designer.html, EVB-IT_digital_Player.html), which are normally transient build outputs that should be gitignored; and binary brand assets (EVB-IT_Logo-2025_v1.2.svg, evb-it_logo.svg) sit loose at the repo root.

naming_conventions:
Score (avg): 4.0
[QWEN] Question evaluated: Does the project use consistent naming conventions for files and directories? Within each domain the conventions are applied consistently: Vue components are PascalCase files in same-named PascalCase folders (AppButton/AppButton.vue, InspectorQuestionMultiChoice/, VariableSelect/); all ~90 icons are PascalCase with an Icon suffix (AddIcon.vue … TrashIcon.vue); all end-to-end specs end in .cy.ts with kebab-case fixture JSON (questionnaire-preview.cy.ts, three-multi-choice-questions.json); component-internal files follow a uniform pattern (types.ts, lib.ts, forms.ts, *.stories.ts); domain code is kebab-case (render-pipeline.ts, migrate-document-page-margin.ts, v1-to-v2-playbook.migration.ts); and test fixtures use a .fixture.ts suffix (base.fixture.ts, playbook.fixture.ts). However, there are visible cross-cutting inconsistencies that prevent a 5: unit-test suffixes mix .spec.ts (AppDialog.spec.ts, dialog.spec.ts, most files) with .test.ts (AppExpressionInput/lib.test.ts) and compound forms (v1-to-v2-playbook.migration.spec.ts); utility naming splits between hyphenated files in src/utils (string-utils.ts, version-utils.ts) and dotted files in src/lib/core/utils (block.util.ts, library.util.ts, zod.util.ts); Pinia stores mix suffixed names (block.store.ts, library.store.ts, settings.store.ts) with unsuffixed ones (layout.ts); root brand assets use conflicting schemes (EVB-IT_Logo-2025_v1.2.svg vs evb-it_logo.svg); cypress/support mixes commands.e2e.ts / component-index.html / e2e.ts; and node-view-props-composible.ts contains a typo ("composible"). Overall: strong per-domain consistency with a handful of systemic lapses.

separation_of_concerns:
Score (avg): 5.0
[QWEN] Question evaluated: Does the project properly separate different concerns into appropriate directories? Yes, with an exemplary layered architecture. Presentation is split from logic: src/components (reusable UI, including App* primitives, inspector panels, modals, question types, TipTap node views) versus src/views (route-level screens further split into creator/, player/, verification/, and shared/ to match the three entry points). State management (src/stores), routing (src/router), internationalization (src/i18n with locales/ and primevue/), and app configuration (src/config) are each isolated. The strongest separation is in the domain layer: src/lib/core contains business logic (types/, interfaces/, constructors/, validators/, migrations/, services/ for conditions/expressions/lookup/render-pipeline/render-template) completely decoupled from src/lib/adapters, which isolates external concerns (api/, docx/ builder and templates, repositories/ with interchangeable local-storage.ts and memory-storage.ts, window/) — a clean, testable hexagonal-style boundary. Tests are separated from product code: all e2e tests, fixtures, and support commands live under cypress/ (with helpers themselves split by concern: questionActions.ts, surveyActions.ts, playbookActions.ts, navigationActions.ts, datatable.ts), while unit-test fixtures are isolated in src/test/ and per-component __fixtures__/ folders. Generated code is quarantined in src/generated/ (player-shell.ts, verification-shell.ts) and produced by scripts/write-player-shell.js, so it never mixes with hand-written source. Static assets sit in src/assets and public/. Minor blemishes (test data in public/ — test-invalid-playbook.json, unit tests co-located rather than in a dedicated tests/ directory, and three util-ish locations: src/utils, src/lib/core/utils, src/composition) do not materially weaken the otherwise thorough separation.

modularity:
Score (avg): 5.0
[QWEN] Question evaluated: Does the project demonstrate good modularity with a logical breakdown of components or modules? The breakdown is consistently modular at every layer. Component level: each of the ~50 component folders is self-contained with its .vue file plus optional types.ts, lib.ts, forms.ts, co-located spec, and .stories.ts (AppButton/, AppRichTextEditor/, VariableSelect/ with its own __fixtures__/ and __snapshots__/). Feature level: question types follow a uniform, extensible trio pattern (QuestionFreeText.vue + QuestionFreeTextForm.vue + QuestionFreeTextPreview.vue, repeated for SingleChoice, MultiChoice, Table, etc.), and inspector panels are one module per entity type (InspectorQuestionSingleChoice, InspectorParamBlock, InspectorDocument with its own panel components). Domain level: migrations are individual versioned modules each with its own spec (migrate-document-page-margin.ts/.spec.ts, v1-to-v2-playbook.migration.ts), validators are per-entity (block.ts, playbook.ts, library.ts, visual-condition.ts), and services are decomposed (conditions/, expressions/, lookup/, render-pipeline.ts, render-template/, deletion/). The rich-text editor is modularized into independent TipTap extensions (IfBlocks/, IfMarks/, ContentPlaceholder/, CustomTable/, CustomImage/, SurveyFingerprintPlaceholder/, Page/, etc.), each pairing an Extension.ts with its Vue node view. Product level: a single codebase is modularly split into three deployable applications (creator, player, verification) with per-mode entry files, router modules (creator.ts, player.ts, verification.ts), and stores (block.store.ts, playbook.store.ts, survey.store.ts, verification.store.ts). Cypress support commands are similarly modularized by domain, and barrel files (icons/index.ts, AppDefinition/index.ts, TipTapExtensions/common.ts) control import surfaces. Minor notes: the components/ directory is large (~50 folders) and utility logic is distributed across src/utils, src/lib/core/utils, and src/composition — but each cluster is cohesive and the overall decomposition is logical and scalable.
